title: Partner ops snapshot — model routing incident and customer-facing summary
content:
Snapshot: quick customer message + post-incident summary (partner ops draft)

Audience: integrator partners and enterprise customers that were routed to fallbacks during Dec 20 EU routing disturbance. This doc is a concise status-page style update suitable for posting to status.redwood.ai and for sending as a partner email/thread.

High-level summary (to publish on status page):
On 2029-12-20 at ~10:37 UTC we observed an automated routing controller mis-evaluating capacity signals for the EU region. A subset of requests were redirected to a lower-capacity model variant as an automated fallback. The fallback path served traffic with increased average latency and, in some cases, reduced structured-output fidelity. We mitigated the issue by rolling back the routing controller policy and gradually restoring normal routes; full recovery occurred by 2029-12-20 12:05 UTC.

Impact:
- Affected customers: ~2.6% of hosted API requests originating from EU control plane region between 10:37–12:05 UTC.
- Symptoms: higher 95th/99th percentile latency (streaming and non-streaming), intermittent truncated structured output for function-call/JSON schema responses, and a small increase in model hallucination rates for long-context prompts sent to fallback variant.
- Duration: 1h28m (partial) with staggered recovery as routes reconciled.

What happened (technical summary):
- The routing controller consumes capacity signals (GPU utilization, queue length, per-tenant token budget). A recently deployed change to the controller's compatibility check for quantized model variants caused a false-negative on compatibility for the primary model pool in EU.
- Because of the compatibility check failure, the controller considered the primary pool unavailable and activated the fallback policy which routes to a smaller/quantized model family with different tokenizer/decoding defaults.
- The fallback model family is production-safe for throughput but demonstrates occasional structured-output mismatches for certain schema-based prompts and slightly higher tail latency under concurrent streaming sessions.

Immediate mitigations performed: timeline (customer-facing phrasing)
- 10:37 UTC: Alert triggered when routing anomaly threshold breached. Internal notif to on-call and routing owners.
- 10:41 UTC: We paused the new compatibility check rollout and reverted the controller config to the last known-good policy for EU.
- 10:55 UTC: Began targeted route reconciliation; manually re-queued impacted shards for the primary model pool.
- 11:22 UTC: Verified decreasing fallback traffic and improved latencies for some tenants. Continued phased reconciliation to avoid capacity thrash.
- 12:05 UTC: Traffic fully returned to primary model pool; monitoring shows latency and quality metrics returned to baseline by 12:15 UTC.

Customer-facing assurances (what customers need to know):
- No customer data was exfiltrated or altered. All requests were processed by Redwood models; the issue was routing to a different model variant, not a data integrity event.
- We do not expect this to have created new persistent state in tenant applications. If you rely on structured JSON outputs, please run a small verification test suite against recent outputs if you observed anomalies.
- For teams using deterministic parsing of model-produced JSON or function call outputs: temporary tokenization differences may have introduced field ordering or escaping changes. Those cases are rare but worth validating.

Actionable guidance (short checklist for customers):
- If you saw higher latency or truncated responses, re-run stalled requests where safe.
- For mission-critical structured outputs, validate the last 100 calls from 10:30–12:30 UTC. If you identify malformed JSON or missing fields, contact support and include the request IDs/time window.
- If you use pinned model versions or explicit model names in requests, this incident should not have changed pins; only requests that depended on routing policies were affected.

Root cause and why it wasn't automatically blocked:
- The compatibility check change was intended to be stricter to avoid running untested quantized paths, but an off-by-one in the model-architecture mapping table led to a mismatch for one primary model version. Because the change passed unit tests and internal canaries (which had different sample distributions), it deployed without triggering a rollback. Our canary sampling did not include the EU workload pattern that exposed the issue.

Planned long-term fixes and timelines:
- Short (0–2 weeks): add a targeted canary that mirrors EU traffic pattern to the routing controller's rollout pipeline; add a synthetic test that validates tokenizer/decoder compatibility across known variants. ETA: 2029-12-31.
- Medium (2–6 weeks): implement an automatic verification step that compares a small batch of schema-string outputs between primary and fallback variants during any live fallback before routing completes. ETA: 2029-01-15.
- Long (6–12 weeks): improve the routing controller logic to prefer capacity-preserving rebalancing over model-family fallback where possible; enhance fallback model families with stricter schema validation hooks. ETA: 2029-02-28.

Compensation and SLA notes:
- We are evaluating the incident against contracted SLAs for affected tenants and will proactively reach out to customers whose usage and SLOs were impacted with proposed credit calculations. Expect outreach from customer-success within 5 business days.

Partner FAQ (for reseller/partner support teams):
Q: Did the fallback change model outputs permanently?
A: No. The change affected only in-flight requests during the incident window. Outputs produced during the window may need verification; there is no persistent change to your pinned model configurations.

Q: Will enabling model pins prevent this?
A: Pinning models avoids routing-based fallbacks in most cases. However, pinned models may still experience higher latency if the chosen pool lacks capacity; pinning is a strong mitigation for quality consistency but affects resilience tradeoffs.

Q: What to provide to support?
A: Request IDs (if available), approximate timestamps, tenant name, and a short description of the symptom (latency, truncated JSON, hallucination).

Next steps for us (internal companion actions):
- Post the status-page summary above and schedule a partner email for impacted enterprise customers.
- Compile example request IDs and a short symptom matrix to send to the engineering owners for triage.
- Track SLA impact and coordinate credit proposals with finance.

Draft status and publishing guidance:
- This draft is approved for partner ops review. After edits by routing owners and legal review for SLA language, prepare two assets: 1) a concise statuspage entry (one-paragraph + timeline + impact bullets) and 2) a longer partner email with verification checklist.

Contact and escalation:
- Primary contact: Mariana Lopez (customer-success) — mariana.lopez@redwood.ai
- Routing owner: Ethan Park — ethan.park@redwood.ai
- On-call lead: Sana Rahman — sana.rahman@redwood.ai

Appendix: short internal timeline (for reference)
- 10:30 UTC: small routing inconsistencies begin as rolling controller push finishes
- 10:37 UTC: alert threshold crossed, fallback policy triggered for subset of shards
- 10:41 UTC: rollback of compatibility check rollout
- 10:55 UTC: manual shard reconciliation starts
- 11:22 UTC: measurable decline in fallback traffic
- 12:05 UTC: primary routes restored
- 12:15 UTC: monitoring baseline reconfirmed

End of draft.

Notes to self: include a short JSON example in the partner email showing the kind of tokenization difference we saw (escape vs unescaped newline) and decide whether to include example request IDs in the public status page or only in partner emails.
